title: Udayin's advice
hookLine: a friend urges him to enjoy life while he's young; the prince answers about aging (Buddhacarita 4)

lines: THE FRIEND WHO TAKES YOU ASIDE.
cards: Look, I'm saying this because I care. You're too serious. Relax.
You've got your whole life for the heavy stuff. In the garden, the friend who takes the prince aside is Udayin, the son of the king's priest, a young man the prince knows well.
He has watched the women try and fail, so he makes the case for pleasure himself. It's a good case. The poem lets him make it fully, and that's what makes the prince's answer worth hearing.

teach.b: First, the argument. Udayin speaks frankly, as a friend. Even if your heart isn't in it, he says, be courteous to these women; turning away from them is unkind.
Then he reaches for old stories: great sages of the past were won over by love and pleasure, so why should you hold out?
And his last point is the one friends still make: enjoy these things now, while you're young. There's time later for the forest. Second, how the prince listens.

He lets Udayin finish, all of it, and when he answers, he starts by granting what's true in it. Third, the answer. In the poem, paraphrased here, the prince says: I don't despise the pleasures of the world.
I know people are bound up in them. But I keep remembering that it all passes. Age is coming, and sickness, and death.
If those three weren't real, I too would find delight here. Because they are, my heart can't settle into it.

teach.h: NOT WICKED. IT JUST DOESN'T LAST.
teach.b: Not that pleasure is wicked: that it doesn't last, and he can't unsee it. Fourth, the tone.
He answers without contempt, and even turns the advice around: if Udayin is truly his friend, why urge him toward what will end, instead of helping him find what won't?
A disagreement between friends, with no one stomping off.
And the king's plan fails again.

how: Some Buddhist teachers describe sense pleasures as impermanent rather than evil in themselves, and this conversation can be retold as an example of disagreeing with kindness.

o: a friend's urging to enjoy pleasure while young
a priest's counsel to marry and rule well
a sage's warning to leave the palace at once

games.q: Udayin and the prince: tap the pairs.
p: it all passes, and I remember that

s: the prince tells Udayin pleasure is wicked
he says he doesn't despise it; it just doesn't last.
Udayin points to great sages of old who gave in to love
he uses the old stories to argue the prince should too.
the prince storms off in anger
he answers gently, as one friend to another.

games.q: a close friend tells you you're too serious and should enjoy life while you're young. you see it differently. what do you do?
o: take his point seriously and answer it kindly.
games.why: the prince says he doesn't despise pleasure, but age, sickness and death are real, and he can't forget them.

practice: Let a voice make its case in your head, a friend's, a relative's, your own: why so serious, have fun, you only live once. Hear it out without interrupting, and notice what's true in it.
If an answer comes, let it come the way the prince's did, without contempt: I hear you, and here's what I keep remembering.

wordCard.voice: Udayin's advice. A friend urges the prince to enjoy pleasure while he's young; the prince answers that it all passes, and he can't forget it. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: desire, pleasure, love; what Udayin urges the prince to enjoy.

carryVoice: Your line: he answered gently. A good argument, kindly heard, kindly declined. Day seven hundred four.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 4 (Udayin's speech and the prince's reply)
